danish.title: Fjerde bog (1806) — Kapitel 4
paragraphs: Pierre sad over for Dolokhov og Nikolaj Rostov. Som sædvanlig spiste og drak han meget og ivrigt. Men de, der kendte ham godt, lagde mærke til, at en stor forandring var sket med ham den dag. Han var tavs under hele middagen, så sig omkring, kneb øjnene sammen og rynkede panden, eller sad med stift blik og et udtryk af fuldstændig åndsfraværelse og gned sig på næseryggen. Hans ansigt var nedtrykt og mørkt. Han syntes hverken at se eller høre, hvad der foregik omkring ham, og var helt optaget af en trykkende og uløst gåde.

Den uløste gåde, der plagede ham, skyldtes hentydninger fra fyrstinden, hans kusine, i Moskva angående Dolokhov's forhold til hans kone, og et anonymt brev, han havde modtaget den morgen. Brevet var skrevet med den lave, spøgende tone, der er typisk for anonyme breve, og fortalte ham, at han ganske vist så dårligt gennem sine briller, men at hans kones forbindelse med Dolokhov var en hemmelighed for alle undtagen ham selv. Pierre troede absolut ikke på hverken fyrstindens hentydninger eller brevet, men han frygtede nu at se på Dolokhov, der sad over for ham. Hver gang han tilfældigvis mødte Dolokhov's kønne, frække øjne, følte Pierre noget frygteligt og uhyrligt rejse sig i hans sjæl og vendte hurtigt blikket væk. Ufrivilligt huskede han sin kones fortid og hendes forhold til Dolokhov, og Pierre indså klart, at det, der stod i brevet, godt kunne være sandt, eller i det mindste synes sandt, hvis det ikke drejede sig om netop hans kone. Han mindedes ufrivilligt, hvordan Dolokhov, der efter felttoget fuldstændig havde genvundet sin tidligere stilling, var vendt tilbage til Petersborg og opsøgt ham. Dolokhov havde, idet han udnyttede sit venskabelige forhold til Pierre som selskabskammerat, opsøgt ham direkte i hans hjem, og Pierre havde givet ham husly og lånt ham penge. Pierre mindedes, hvordan Helene (hans kone) smilende havde udtrykt sin misbilligelse af, at Dolokhov boede i deres hus, og hvordan Dolokhov kynisk havde rost hans kones skønhed for ham og fra den tid til deres ankomst i Moskva ikke havde forladt dem en eneste dag.

»Ja, han er meget smuk,« tænkte Pierre, »og jeg kender ham. Det ville være ham en særlig fornøjelse at vanære mit navn og gøre nar af mig, netop fordi jeg har anstrengt mig for ham, taget mig af ham og hjulpet ham. Ja, jeg ved og forstår, hvilken ekstra krydderi det ville give glæden ved at bedrage mig, hvis det virkelig var sandt. Ja, hvis det var sandt, men det tror jeg ikke. Jeg har ingen ret til at tro det og kan ikke tro det.« Han mindedes det udtryk, Dolokhov's ansigt antog i hans grusomme øjeblikke — da han bandt politibetjenten til bjørnen og kastede dem i vandet, eller da han udfordrede en mand til duel uden grund, eller skød en postkusks hest med en pistol. Det udtryk lå ofte i Dolokhov's ansigt, når han så på Pierre. »Ja, han er en bølle,« tænkte Pierre, »at dræbe et menneske betyder intet for ham. Han må føle, at alle er bange for ham, og det må behage ham. Han må tro, at jeg også er bange for ham — og i virkeligheden er jeg bange for ham,« tænkte han, og igen følte han noget frygteligt og uhyrligt rejse sig i sin sjæl. Dolokhov, Denisov og Rostov sad nu over for Pierre og var tilsyneladende i strålende humør. Rostov talte muntert med sine to venner, en flot husar og en berygtet duellant og livsnyder, og sendte af og til et ironisk blik mod Pierre, hvis optagne, adspredte og vældige skikkelse var meget iøjnefaldende ved middagen. Rostov så uvenligt på Pierre, for det første fordi Pierre i en husars øjne var en rig civilist, en smuk kvindes ægtemand, kort sagt en kælling; og for det andet fordi Pierre i sin adspredte åndsfraværelse ikke havde genkendt Rostov og ikke besvaret hans hilsen. Da der blev drukket for kejserens sundhed, tog Pierre, fordybet i tanker, hverken sit glas eller rejste sig.
»Hvad laver De dog?« råbte Rostov i et anfald af raseri. »Hører De ikke? Det er Hans Majestæt Kejserens skål!«
Pierre sukkede, rejste sig lydig, tømte sit glas, og da alle igen var sat ned, vendte han sig med sit godmodige smil til Rostov.
»Jamen, jeg genkendte Dem ikke!« sagde han. Men Rostov var optaget af andet; han råbte »Hurra!«
»Hvorfor fornyer du ikke bekendtskabet?« sagde Dolokhov til Rostov.
»Pyt med ham, han er en tåbe!« sagde Rostov.
»Man bør pleje de smukke kvinders ægtemænd,« sagde Denisov.
Pierre hørte ikke, hvad de sagde, men vidste, at de talte om ham. Han rødmede og vendte sig bort.
»Nå, så lad os drikke for de smukke kvinders sundhed!« sagde Dolokhov, og med en alvorlig mine, men med et smil lurende i mundvigene, vendte han sig med sit glas mod Pierre.
»For de smukke kvinders sundhed, Peterkin — og deres elskere!« tilføjede han.

Pierre drak med sænket blik af sit glas uden at se på Dolokhov eller svare ham. Lakajen, der uddelte blade med Kutuzovs kantate, lagde et foran Pierre som en af hovedgæsterne. Han var lige ved at tage det, da Dolokhov lænede sig henover bordet, snuppede det fra hans hånd og begyndte at læse det. Pierre stirrede på Dolokhov, og hans øjne sænkedes, og det forfærdelige og uhyrlige, der havde plaget ham hele middagen, rejste sig og tog magten over ham. Han lænede hele sin vældige krop henover bordet.
»Vov De at tage det?« råbte han.
Da Nesvitskij og hans sidemand hørte råbet og så, hvem det var rettet mod, vendte de sig forskrækket mod Bezukhov.
»Lad være! Lad dog være! Hvad laver De?« hviskede deres forskræmte stemmer.
Dolokhov så på Pierre med klare, muntre, grusomme øjne og det smil, der syntes at sige: »Ah, det er dét, jeg kan lide!«
»Det får De ikke!« sagde han tydeligt.
Pierre, bleg og med skælvende læber, rev kopien til sig.
»De ... De ... slyngel! Jeg udfordrer Dem!« udstødte han og skubbede stolen tilbage og rejste sig fra bordet.

I det selvsamme øjeblik, da han gjorde dette og sagde de ord, følte Pierre, at spørgsmålet om hans kones skyld, der havde martret ham hele dagen, endegyldigt og uigenkaldeligt var besvaret bekræftende. Han hadede hende og var for evigt adskilt fra hende. Trods Denisovs bøn om, at han ikke ville blande sig i sagen, indvilligede Rostov i at være Dolokhov's sekundant, og efter middagen drøftede han duelaftalerne med Nesvitskij, Bezukhovs sekundant. Pierre tog hjem, mens Rostov med Dolokhov og Denisov blev i klubben til sent og lyttede til sigøjnersangerne og andre musikanter.
»Godt, så ses vi i morgen ved Sokolniki,« sagde Dolokhov, da han tog afsked med Rostov i klubbens forhal.
»Og føler du dig helt rolig?« spurgte Rostov.
Dolokhov standsede.

»Jamen ser du, jeg skal fortælle dig hele hemmeligheden bag dueller med to ord. Hvis du skal slås i en duel og skriver testamente og kærlige breve til dine forældre, og hvis du tænker, at du måske bliver dræbt, er du en tåbe og tabt på forhånd. Men gå med den faste beslutning om at dræbe din mand så hurtigt og sikkert som muligt, og så skal det hele nok gå. Sådan sagde vores bjørnejæger i Kostroma altid til mig: 'Alle er bange for bjørnen,' sagde han, 'men når du ser en, er al frygten væk, og du tænker kun på ikke at lade den slippe!' Og sådan har jeg det. À demain, mon cher.« *
* Til i morgen, min kære ven.

Næste dag, klokken otte om morgenen, kørte Pierre og Nesvitskij til Sokolniki-skoven og fandt Dolokhov, Denisov og Rostov allerede på pletten. Pierre havde udseende af en mand, der var optaget af tanker, som intet havde med sagen at gøre. Hans udmarvede ansigt var gult. Han havde tilsyneladende ikke sovet den nat. Han så sig adspredt om og kneb øjnene sammen, som blændet af solen. Han var fuldstændig optaget af to overvejelser: sin kones skyld, som han efter den søvnløse nat ikke nærede den mindste tvivl om, og Dolokhov's uskyldighed, der ingen grund havde til at værne om en mands ære, som intet betød for ham ... »Jeg ville nok have gjort det samme i hans sted,« tænkte Pierre. »Det er ligefrem sikkert, at jeg ville have gjort det samme, og hvorfor så denne duel, dette mord? Enten dræber jeg ham, eller også rammer han mig i hovedet, albuen eller knæet. Kan jeg ikke bare gå herfra, stikke af, gemme mig et sted?« passerede gennem hans tanker. Men netop i de øjeblikke, hvor sådanne tanker kom, spurgte han med en ejendommelig ro og adspredt ligegyldighed, der indgød de tilstedeværende respekt: »Varer det endnu længe? Er alt klar?«
Da alt var parat, sablerne stukket ned i sneen for at markere barriererne, og pistolerne ladet, gik Nesvitskij hen til Pierre.

»Jeg ville svigte min pligt, greve,« sagde han med sky stemme, »og ikke retfærdiggøre Deres tillid og den ære, De har vist mig ved at vælge mig som Deres sekundant, hvis jeg i dette alvorlige, dette yderst alvorlige øjeblik ikke sagde Dem hele sandheden. Jeg mener, der er ingen tilstrækkelig grund til denne affære, eller til at der udgydes blod ... De havde ikke ret, ikke helt ret, De var ubesindig ...«
»Å ja, det er frygteligt dumt,« sagde Pierre.

»Tillad mig da at udtrykke Deres beklagelse, og jeg er sikker på, Deres modstander vil tage imod den,« sagde Nesvitskij (der ligesom de andre involverede, og som alle i lignende tilfælde, endnu ikke troede, at det virkelig ville komme til en duel). »De ved, greve, det er langt ærefuldt at indrømme sin fejl end at lade tingene gå så langt, at de ikke kan gøres om. Der var ingen fornærmelse fra nogen af siderne. Tillad mig at forhandle ...«
»Nej! Hvad er der at tale om?« sagde Pierre. »Det er helt lige meget ... Er alt parat? Fortæl mig bare, hvor jeg skal stå, og hvor jeg skal skyde,« sagde han med et unaturligt venligt smil.
Han tog pistolen i hånden og begyndte at spørge om aftrækkeren, da han aldrig før havde holdt en pistol i hånden — et faktum, han ikke ønskede at indrømme.
»Åh ja, sådan, det ved jeg, jeg havde bare glemt det,« sagde han.
»Ingen undskyldning, ingen overhovedet,« sagde Dolokhov til Denisov, der på sin side også havde forsøgt en forsoning, og han gik ligeledes hen til sin plads.

Stedet, der var valgt til duellen, var en rydning i fyrreskovens omkring firs alen fra vejen, hvor slæderne holdt, dækket af smeltende sne, da frosten var begyndt at slippe de seneste dage. Modstanderne stod fyrre skridt fra hinanden ved rydningens yderste kant. Sekundanterne, der afmålte skridtene, efterlod spor i den dybe, våde sne mellem de steder, hvor de havde stået, og Nesvitskijs og Dolokhov's sabler, der var stukket i jorden ti skridt fra hinanden for at markere barriererne. Det tøede, og der lå dis; på fyrre skridts afstand kunne man intet se. I tre minutter havde alt været klart, men de tøvede stadig, og alle var tavse.

english.title: Book Four (1806) — Chapter 4
paragraphs: Pierre sat across from Dolokhov and Nicholas Rostov. As usual, he ate and drank heavily. But those who knew him well could see that some great change had come over him that day. He was silent throughout dinner, looking around while blinking and frowning, or else staring into space with complete absent-mindedness, rubbing the bridge of his nose. His face was gloomy and troubled. He seemed to see and hear nothing happening around him, entirely absorbed by some painful, unresolved problem.

The problem tormenting him had been set in motion by hints from the princess — his cousin — in Moscow, regarding Dolokhov's intimacy with his wife, and by an anonymous letter he had received that morning. The letter, written in the typically crude and mocking style of such messages, said that he couldn't see well through his spectacles, but that his wife's affair with Dolokhov was a secret to no one but him. Pierre categorically refused to believe either the princess's hints or the letter, but he now dreaded looking at Dolokhov, who sat right across from him. Every time he accidentally met Dolokhov's handsome, insolent eyes, Pierre felt something terrible and monstrous rising in his soul and quickly turned away. Involuntarily recalling his wife's past and her relationship with Dolokhov, Pierre could see clearly that what the letter described might be true — or at least could appear true — if it hadn't been about his own wife. He couldn't help remembering how Dolokhov, who had fully recovered his former standing after the campaign, had returned to Petersburg and come to him. Taking advantage of their friendship as drinking companions, Dolokhov had moved straight into Pierre's house, and Pierre had put him up and lent him money. Pierre recalled how Helene had smiled disapprovingly at Dolokhov living with them, and how Dolokhov had brazenly complimented Pierre on his wife's beauty — and from that point on, all the way to Moscow, had never left them for a single day.

"Yes, he's very handsome," thought Pierre, "and I know his character. It would give him special pleasure to dishonor my name and humiliate me, precisely because I've gone out of my way for him — befriended him, helped him. I know and understand how much extra relish that would add to the pleasure of deceiving me, if it were really true. Yes, if it were true — but I don't believe it. I have no right to believe it, and I can't." He remembered the expression Dolokhov's face took on in moments of cruelty — when he had tied a policeman to a bear and dropped them into the water, when he had challenged a man to a duel for no reason, when he had shot a coachman's horse with a pistol. That expression was often on Dolokhov's face when he looked at Pierre. "Yes, he's a thug," thought Pierre. "Killing a man means nothing to him. He must think everyone's afraid of him, and that must please him. He probably thinks I'm afraid of him too — and in fact, I am." And again he felt something terrible and monstrous rising within him. Dolokhov, Denisov, and Rostov were sitting across from Pierre and seemed to be in high spirits. Rostov was talking cheerfully with his two friends — one a dashing hussar, the other a notorious duelist and libertine — and he kept glancing mockingly at Pierre, whose preoccupied, distracted, and massive figure was quite conspicuous at the dinner. Rostov regarded Pierre with hostility — first, because in a hussar's eyes Pierre was merely a rich civilian married to a beauty, in other words, an old woman; and second, because Pierre, lost in his own thoughts, hadn't recognized Rostov or returned his greeting. When the toast to the Emperor's health was drunk, Pierre, deep in thought, didn't stand or raise his glass.
"What are you doing?" shouted Rostov, staring at him in an ecstasy of indignation. "Don't you hear? It's His Majesty the Emperor's health!"
Pierre sighed, stood up obediently, emptied his glass, and after everyone had sat down again, turned to Rostov with his usual kind smile.
"I'm sorry — I didn't recognize you!" he said. But Rostov was already occupied with something else — he was shouting "Hurrah!"
"Why don't you go reintroduce yourself?" said Dolokhov to Rostov.
"Forget him — he's an idiot," said Rostov.
"One should make an effort with the husbands of pretty women," said Denisov.
Pierre didn't catch what they were saying, but he knew they were talking about him. He turned red and looked away.
"Well then — to the health of beautiful women!" said Dolokhov, and with a serious expression but a smile lurking at the corners of his mouth, he raised his glass toward Pierre.
"To the health of lovely women, my dear Petrusha — and their lovers!" he added.

Pierre, eyes downcast, drained his glass without looking at Dolokhov or responding. A footman distributing copies of Kutuzov's cantata placed one in front of Pierre as one of the principal guests. He was about to pick it up when Dolokhov leaned across the table and snatched it from his hand, starting to read it. Pierre stared at Dolokhov, and his eyes darkened. The terrible, monstrous thing that had been tormenting him all through dinner surged up and took hold of him. He heaved his massive body across the table.
"How dare you take that!" he shouted.
Hearing that shout and seeing who it was directed at, Nesvitski and the man sitting beside Pierre turned to him in alarm.
"Stop! Stop! What are you doing?" came their frightened whispers.
Dolokhov looked at Pierre with clear, amused, cruel eyes, wearing that smile of his that seemed to say, "Ah, now this is what I enjoy."
"You won't have it," he said distinctly.
Pierre, white-faced, his lips trembling, grabbed the copy back.
"You... you... scoundrel! I challenge you!" he burst out, and shoving back his chair, he rose from the table.

At the very instant he said those words, Pierre felt that the question of his wife's guilt — which had been torturing him all day — was finally and conclusively answered: yes, she was guilty. He hated her and was forever separated from her. Despite Denisov's plea that he stay out of it, Rostov agreed to serve as Dolokhov's second. After dinner, he discussed the arrangements for the duel with Nesvitski, who was Pierre's second. Pierre went home, but Rostov, Dolokhov, and Denisov stayed on at the club until late, listening to the gypsy singers and other performers.
"So then — tomorrow at Sokolniki," said Dolokhov, taking leave of Rostov at the club entrance.
"And you feel completely calm?" Rostov asked.
Dolokhov paused.

"I'll tell you the whole secret of dueling in two words. If you're going to fight a duel and you sit down to write your will and tender letters to your parents, thinking you might be killed — you're a fool and you're done for. But if you go with the firm intention of killing your opponent as quickly and surely as possible, then everything will be fine. That's what our bear hunter back in Kostroma used to tell me: 'Everyone's afraid of a bear,' he'd say, 'but once you see one, all your fear vanishes — your only thought is not to let him get away!' That's how it is with me. [speaking in French] Till tomorrow, my dear fellow."
* Till tomorrow, my dear fellow.

The next morning, at eight o'clock, Pierre and Nesvitski drove to the Sokolniki forest, where they found Dolokhov, Denisov, and Rostov already waiting. Pierre had the look of a man consumed by thoughts that had nothing to do with the matter at hand. His drawn face was sallow. He had obviously not slept. He kept looking around distractedly and squinting as if dazzled by the sun. He was entirely preoccupied with two thoughts: his wife's guilt, of which he no longer had the slightest doubt after his sleepless night, and the blamelessness of Dolokhov, who had no reason to protect the honor of a man who meant nothing to him. "I would probably have done the same in his place," Pierre thought. "Actually, I'm sure I would have. So why this duel? Why this killing? Either I'll kill him, or he'll hit me in the head, or the elbow, or the knee. Why can't I just leave — run away — disappear somewhere?" Such thoughts kept passing through his mind. But at those very moments he would ask, in a particularly calm, distracted tone that earned the respect of the onlookers, "Will this take much longer? Is everything ready?"
When everything was prepared — the sabers planted in the snow to mark the barriers and the pistols loaded — Nesvitski walked up to Pierre.

"I would not be doing my duty, Count," he said in a timid voice, "and would not deserve the confidence and honor you've shown me by choosing me as your second, if at this grave — this very grave — moment, I did not tell you the whole truth. I believe there are no sufficient grounds for this affair, and no reason for blood to be shed. You were not entirely right — you were impulsive..."
"Oh yes, it's horribly stupid," said Pierre.

"Then allow me to convey your regrets, and I'm sure your opponent will accept them," said Nesvitski, who, like everyone else involved — and like everyone in such situations — still couldn't quite believe it had come to an actual duel. "You know, Count, it's far more honorable to admit a mistake than to let things become irreparable. There was no real insult on either side. Let me speak to them..."
"No! What is there to discuss?" said Pierre. "It doesn't matter.... Is everything ready?" he added. "Just tell me where to stand and where to aim." He said this with an unnaturally gentle smile.
He took the pistol and began asking how the trigger worked, since he had never held a pistol before — a fact he didn't want to admit.
"Oh yes, that's right — I know. I just forgot," he said.
"No apologies — none whatsoever," said Dolokhov to Denisov, who had been attempting a reconciliation on his side. Then Dolokhov too walked to his appointed place.

The spot chosen for the duel was about eighty paces from the road where the sleighs had been left — a small clearing in the pine forest, covered in melting snow, the frost having broken during the past few days. The two men stood forty paces apart at the far edge of the clearing. The seconds paced out the distance, leaving tracks in the deep, wet snow between the starting positions and the two sabers stuck in the ground ten paces apart to mark the barriers. The air was damp and misty. At forty paces, nothing could be seen clearly. For three minutes everything had been ready, but still they delayed, and everyone was silent.
